title: The Dream of the Rood
description: The greatest religious poem of the Old English period (156 lines): a dream vision in which the Cross itself speaks, recounting the Crucifixion as a heroic battle in which Christ, the young warrior-king, mounts the cross of his own will. Related texts survive on the eighth-century Ruthwell Cross runic inscription and the Brussels Cross.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer sees a wondrous tree shining with gold and gems, stained with blood, and the Rood tells its story: cut down in the forest, it was made the gallows of the young hero who climbed it willingly; it trembled, dared not bow, and with Christ it was pierced with nails and mocked, then buried and later raised up as the honoured sign of salvation. The poem ends with the dreamer's hope of the heavenly homeland and the injunction to seek the tree of victory.
narrative_structure: A frame vision enclosing the Cross's first-person narrative, followed by the dreamer's response and a homiletic conclusion; the Cross is the earliest sustained prosopopoeia in English poetry.
principal_characters: the Dreamer; the Rood (Cross); Christ (the young hero)
literary_form: dream vision in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre, richly figured; the poem's end has been thought to show hypermetric lines.
historical_context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII, fols. 104v-106r); the Ruthwell Cross (Dumfriesshire, early eighth century) carries an inscribed extract in runes, and the Brussels Cross (c. 1000) a related couplet, evidence of the poem's early circulation.
literary_significance: The supreme fusion of Germanic heroic form with Christian content in the period; one of the great medieval dream poems.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; early attributions to Cædmon or Cynewulf are not accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Vercelli Book, fols. 104v-106r; Ruthwell Cross runic inscription; Brussels Cross inscription.

title: The Phoenix
description: An allegorical poem of 677 lines on the legend of the phoenix, which burns itself on its nest of spices and rises renewed: a figure, the poem explains, of the resurrection of the body and the Christian's hope of the heavenly homeland. Based on the Carmen de ave phoenice attributed to Lactantius, it contains one of the finest paradise descriptions in Old English.
plot_or_argument: The poem describes the earthly paradise in the east where the phoenix dwells; after a thousand years the bird flies to Syria, builds a nest of spices, is consumed by fire, and after three days revives from the ashes. The second half interprets the legend allegorically: the phoenix is Christ and the blessed soul, the nest the good works, and the renewal the resurrection at the Last Judgment.
narrative_structure: A bipartite structure of literal legend followed by sustained allegorical exposition (the latter an original expansion of the Latin source).
principal_characters: the Phoenix (as bird and as allegorical figure)
literary_form: allegorical religious narrative in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; the poem is notable for its extended descriptive set-pieces.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the Latin source (fourth century, attributed to Lactantius) circulated widely in Anglo-Saxon England.
literary_significance: The fullest Old English allegory of resurrection and the richest nature-description in the corpus.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 55b-65b.

title: The Panther
description: A poem of 74 lines from the Old English Physiologus group: the panther, fairest of beasts with its dappled coat, sleeps for three days and then calls with a sweet breath that draws all animals except the dragon. The poem allegorizes the panther as Christ, whose death, descent, and resurrection draw all souls — and the dragon as the devil who flees his fragrance.
plot_or_argument: The poem describes the panther's beauty and gentleness, its three-day sleep and awakening, and the sweet breath that gathers the beasts; the interpretation identifies the panther with Christ, the dappled coat with his many virtues, and the sweet breath with the call of the gospel, which the old serpent, the devil, cannot endure.
narrative_structure: Description followed by explicit allegorical interpretation, the standard Physiologus pattern.
principal_characters: the Panther (Christ); the Dragon (the devil)
literary_form: bestiary poetry in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book with The Whale and The Partridge; the Physiologus tradition reached England via Latin intermediaries and remained productive through the Middle Ages.
literary_significance: Part of the earliest English bestiary and of the allegorical natural-history tradition that culminates in the medieval bestiaries.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 95b-96b.

title: The Whale
description: A poem of 89 lines on the legend of the whale (Fastitocalon) that lies like an island: sailors moor to it, light fires, and are dragged down when the beast dives. The poem reads it as an allegory of the devil, who lures sinners with the appearance of safety and plunges them into hell.
plot_or_argument: Mariners mistake the whale's back for an island, anchor and kindle fires; when the creature senses the heat it dives, drowning the crew. The allegory applies the story to the devil, whose deceptive promises — the sweet sins that seem secure ground — drag the unwary soul into the abyss.
narrative_structure: Narrative exemplum followed by allegorical application, in the Physiologus manner.
principal_characters: the Whale (Fastitocalon; the devil); the mariners (sinners)
literary_form: bestiary poetry in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book with The Panther and The Partridge.
literary_significance: The earliest English version of the whale-island legend, later famous in the Navigatio Sancti Brendani and Mandeville; a vivid allegory of temptation.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 96b-97b.

title: The Partridge
description: A poem of 16 lines, the third of the Exeter Book Physiologus group: the partridge, which steals and broods the eggs of other birds, sees its stolen brood desert it when they hatch and hear their true mother's call. The allegory (imperfectly preserved) contrasts the devil's stolen brood with those who hear the true voice of Christ.
plot_or_argument: The partridge hatches eggs not its own; when the chicks hear their real mother they leave the deceiver. The brief application praises those who turn to their true parent — the text breaks off where the interpretation of the fable is developed.
narrative_structure: Fable followed by a broken-off allegorical application.
principal_characters: the Partridge; the stolen brood
literary_form: bestiary poetry in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book, immediately after The Whale.
literary_significance: Completes the earliest English bestiary group.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 97b-98a (incomplete).

title: Judith
description: A fragmentary poem of 349 lines (the opening is lost) retelling the apocryphal Book of Judith: the Hebrew heroine beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes in his tent and rouses her people to victory. The poem recasts the biblical heroine as a figure of the heroic tradition — a maiden of God wielding the sword against the enemies of her people.
plot_or_argument: Judith, beautiful and wise, is brought to the drunken Holofernes's tent; praying for aid, she seizes his sword and strikes off his head in two blows, then carries the head back to Bethulia in a food-bag. At dawn she shows the head to her people and delivers a speech of triumph; the Hebrews attack the leaderless Assyrians, who flee; Judith receives the spoils of Holofernes as her reward, and the poem ends with praise of God.
narrative_structure: Dramatic narrative in the heroic manner: the tent scene, the return, the battle, and the distribution of spoils; the heroine's speeches drive the action.
principal_characters: Judith; Holofernes; the Bethulians
literary_form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre, with vigorous battle diction.
historical_context: Preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv) immediately after Beowulf; the biblical book of Judith was known to the Anglo-Saxons through the Vulgate and Ælfric's later prose homily on the same subject.
literary_significance: The finest Old English poem on a female biblical hero; a masterly fusion of heroic style and devotional purpose.
bibliographical_notes: Nowell Codex, British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv, fols. 202a-209a.

title: Exodus
description: A poem of 590 lines on the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea, from the Junius manuscript: a bravura reworking of Exodus 13-14 in which Moses becomes a heroic leader and the crossing a nautical epic, prefiguring the Christian's passage through the waters of baptism and the harrowing of hell.
plot_or_argument: After a prologue on Moses and the law, the poem narrates the pursuit of the Israelites by Pharaoh's host, the pillar of cloud and fire, the parting of the waters, the drowning of the Egyptians, and the Israelites' division of spoils on the far shore; it closes with an allegorical exegesis of the crossing (the 'keys of the deep', the 'spiritual meanings') and allusions to Noah, Abraham, Solomon's temple, and the end of the world.
narrative_structure: Narrative epic with an extended typological epilogue; the abrupt shifts of scene (Noah, Abraham, the temple) have prompted theories of textual disruption.
principal_characters: Moses; Pharaoh; the Israelites; Abraham; Noah
literary_form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre of unusual density; famous kennings for the sea ('the whale's road', 'the swan's riding-place').
historical_context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 143-171); the poem is often linked with the Cædmonian school of biblical paraphrase mentioned by Bede.
literary_significance: The most stylistically daring of the Old Testament poems; its sea imagery is a high point of Old English diction.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the Cædmonian attribution is traditional only.
bibliographical_notes: Junius manuscript, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11.

title: Genesis A
description: A poem of 2,935 lines paraphrasing Genesis 1-22, from the creation and the fall of the angels to the sacrifice of Isaac. The longest of the Junius manuscript poems, it is the foundational Old Testament epic of the period, composed in the plain style of the 'Cædmonian' school.
plot_or_argument: The poem recounts the fall of the rebel angels, the six days of creation, the fall of Adam and Eve and their expulsion, Cain and Abel, the generations to Noah, the Flood and the covenant, the tower of Babel, and the story of Abraham to the near-sacrifice of Isaac, concluding with the promise of the seed.
narrative_structure: Continuous biblical paraphrase in epic form, with an interpolated passage (Genesis B, lines 235-851) translated from Old Saxon treating the fall in greater detail.
principal_characters: God; Adam; Eve; Satan; Cain; Abel; Noah; Abraham; Sarah; Isaac; Lot
literary_form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre in a relatively plain, narrative style.
historical_context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11); its opening lines were long known as 'Cædmon's Genesis' from the early editor Junius's attribution.
literary_significance: The earliest sustained biblical epic in English; a primary witness to the vernacular reception of scripture.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; attribution to Cædmon is traditional and no longer accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Junius manuscript, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 1-142.

title: Genesis B
description: A poem of 617 lines, interpolated into Genesis A (lines 235-851), translated from an Old Saxon original and containing the most celebrated scenes of the fall in Old English: Satan's proud rebellion ('better for me to be a king in hell'), the temptation of Adam by the disguised tempter, and the grief of Eve.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with Satan's boast against God and his binding in hell; an envoy demon journeys to Eden and, taking the form of a serpent, tempts first Adam (unsuccessfully) and then Eve, deceiving her with the promise of a vision of heaven; Eve eats and persuades Adam; the poem closes on their shame and the beginning of repentance, with the original ending lost in the transition back to Genesis A.
narrative_structure: A dramatic expansion of the fall narrative built on lengthy speeches — Satan's monologue, the tempter's persuasions, Eve's lament — unique in the corpus for its psychological interest.
principal_characters: Satan; the Tempter (demon); Adam; Eve
literary_form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre, with occasional hypermetric lines betraying the Old Saxon original.
historical_context: Translated into Old English from an Old Saxon poem (possibly connected with the ninth-century Heliand milieu) and interpolated into Genesis A in the Junius manuscript; the Old Saxon original survives only in a few Vatican fragments.
literary_significance: Contains the finest dramatic treatment of the fall in early English poetry; its Satan anticipates Milton's in power and pathos, a connection first argued by Sievers in 1875.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the interpolation was first detected by Eduard Sievers (1875).
bibliographical_notes: Junius manuscript, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 13-40 (interpolated into Genesis A); Vatican fragments of the Old Saxon original (Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Pal. lat. 1447).

title: Daniel
description: A poem of 764 lines on the book of Daniel, from the Junius manuscript: the three youths in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, the king's dream of the tree and his madness, and the fall of Babylon to the Medes and Persians under the writing on the wall — with the liturgical Canticles of the three youths (the 'Azarias' material) expanded into songs of praise.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows Daniel and his companions at the Babylonian court; Nebuchadnezzar's idol and the furnace; the king's dream of the great tree, interpreted by Daniel as his own pride and coming fall; his seven years of bestial madness and restoration; Belshazzar's feast, the writing on the wall, and the city's fall to Cyrus. The youths' prayers and songs in the furnace (the Canticum trium puerorum) are rendered as extended lyric passages.
narrative_structure: Episodic biblical narrative punctuated by lyric set-pieces (the canticles), with an admonitory frame on pride and the fall of kings.
principal_characters: Daniel; Nebuchadnezzar; Belshazzar; Azarias, Ananias, and Misael (the three youths); Cyrus
literary_form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; the canticle passages show a more ornate, lyrical style.
historical_context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11); related to the Exeter Book poem Azarias, which preserves a version of the first canticle.
literary_significance: A sustained meditation on pride and the fall of kings, central to the Junius manuscript's providential scheme.
bibliographical_notes: Junius manuscript, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 173-212.

title: Christ and Satan
description: A poem of 729 lines in three parts, closing the Junius manuscript: the lament of the fallen angels in hell, the harrowing of hell and the Resurrection, and the temptation of Christ in the wilderness. Its long speeches of Satan and the fallen host are the most extended 'infernal' passages in Old English.
plot_or_argument: Part I: Satan and his angels bewail their fall and their exile from the light of heaven, in a series of remorseful laments. Part II: the harrowing of hell — Christ's descent to liberate the patriarchs — is narrated together with the Resurrection and Ascension. Part III: the devil tempts the fasting Christ in the desert, and is answered and routed; the poem ends with the Last Judgment.
narrative_structure: Three loosely joined narrative sections on a cosmic theme — fall, redemption, and the final victory — unified by the figure of Satan's defeat.
principal_characters: Satan; the fallen angels; Christ; the devils of the temptation; Eve (in retrospect)
literary_form: religious narrative poetry in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; the style varies sharply between sections, suggesting composite authorship.
historical_context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 213-229); the three parts may be independent poems of different dates gathered by the compiler.
literary_significance: The fullest English treatment of the fallen angels before Milton; its harrowing-of-hell narrative is the classic vernacular statement of the theme.
bibliographical_notes: Junius manuscript, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11.

title: Andreas
description: A poem of 1,722 lines on the apocryphal Acts of Andrew and Matthias: the apostle Andrew, sailing incognito with Christ himself as his helmsman, voyages to the cannibal city of Mermedonia to rescue his fellow apostle Matthew. The poem recasts the apostle as a heroic seafarer in the manner of Beowulf, with some of the corpus's most vivid voyage imagery.
plot_or_argument: Christ, disguised as a ship's captain, ferries the reluctant Andrew over the stormy sea, hearing his preaching on the way; in Mermedonia, Andrew is seized, tortured, and imprisoned, but a flood released from a stone pillar drowns his tormentors and revives them, converting the city; Andrew establishes a church and departs, leaving the poem's didactic epilogue.
narrative_structure: A sea-voyage frame enclosing the martyrdom-and-conversion narrative, with speeches, miracles, and a flood scene modelled on Exodus; the poem borrows formulaic lines directly from Beowulf.
principal_characters: Andrew; Christ (the helmsman); Matthew; the Mermedonians
literary_form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre in the classical heroic manner.
historical_context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 29v-52v); based on a Latin version of the apocryphal Acts, itself known in Old English prose from the Blickling manuscript.
literary_significance: The fullest Old English saint's life in verse and a celebrated example of the heroic adaptation of hagiography.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the Beowulf borrowings are stylistic, not evidence of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: Vercelli Book, Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII, fols. 29v-52v.

title: The Fates of the Apostles
description: A poem of 122 lines cataloguing the deaths and missionary fields of the twelve apostles, signed by Cynewulf in a runic acrostic that spells his name. The catalogue frame encloses a meditation on the poet's own need for grace, the best-known of the four Cynewulfian signatures.
plot_or_argument: The poet, speaking as a weary traveller, enumerates the apostles in order — where each preached and how each died (Peter crucified, Paul beheaded, Andrew in Achaia, John at Ephesus, and so on) — then turns to himself: begging the prayers of the reader, weaving the runes of his name into a meditation on the gifts of God and the terror of judgment.
narrative_structure: A thula-like catalogue of the apostles followed by the runic signature passage, which modulates from report to prayer.
principal_characters: the twelve apostles; the poet (Cynewulf)
literary_form: religious catalogue poem in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; the runic acrostic spells CYNEWULF.
historical_context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 52v-54r) and in the same collection as Andreas and the homilies.
literary_significance: The earliest signature of an English poet in his own verse; a key document for the Cynewulf canon.
attribution_notes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes; accepted as authentic.
bibliographical_notes: Vercelli Book, Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII, fols. 52v-54r.

title: Elene
alternative_titles: The Finding of the True Cross
description: Cynewulf's longest signed poem (1,321 lines), on the legend of the Finding of the True Cross: the empress Helena, mother of Constantine, journeys to Jerusalem, compels the Jews to reveal the site of the Crucifixion, and recovers the cross. The poem is a masterpiece of typological narrative, casting Helena as a heroic queen and the cross as the sign of victory.
plot_or_argument: Constantine, granted a vision of the cross before battle, sends his mother Helena to Jerusalem; her search, the interrogation of the Jew Judas (who resists, is imprisoned, converted by a sign, and baptized as Cyriacus), the miraculous finding of the three crosses, the proof by resurrection of a dead youth, the conversion of the Jews, and Helena's building of churches; the epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature and his meditation on judgment and poetry.
narrative_structure: A conversion narrative in the heroic manner, organized around three debates (Constantine's vision, Helena's interrogations, Judas's conversion) and closing on the runic signature.
principal_characters: Elene (Helena); Constantine; Judas/Cyriacus; Satan (in the debate with Judas)
literary_form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; the signature passage is among the most ornate in the corpus.
historical_context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 121v-133v); based on the Latin Acta Cyriaci tradition of the Inventio crucis legend.
literary_significance: The richest treatment in early English poetry of the cross as sign of victory; the locus classicus of Cynewulf's typological art.
bibliographical_notes: Vercelli Book, Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII, fols. 121v-133v.

title: Juliana
description: Cynewulf's signed poem of 731 lines on the passion of St Juliana of Nicomedia: the virgin martyr who withstands her pagan suitor, defeats a demon sent to tempt her, and endures torture and death. The poem contains the most extended debate between saint and demon in Old English.
plot_or_argument: Juliana refuses to marry the prefect Eleusius unless he converts; denounced by her father, she is beaten, hung by the hair, and thrown in prison, where a demon disguised as an angel urges her to yield; she seizes him and forces him to confess his works, then is subjected to fire and a boiling cauldron, and finally beheaded — her soul received into heaven, her persecutors drowned at sea. The epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature.
narrative_structure: A debate-driven passio: successive confrontations (suitor, father, demon, judge) leading to martyrdom, framed by the demon's confession of the history of evil and the poet's runic prayer.
principal_characters: Juliana; Eleusius; Africanus (her father); the demon; the angel
literary_form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 65b-76v); based on a Latin passio of Juliana.
literary_significance: The classic Old English virgin-martyr poem and the fullest statement of the saint-demon debate.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 65b-76v.

title: Christ I (The Advent Lyrics)
description: The first part of the Exeter Book 'Christ' trilogy: twelve Advent lyrics (439 lines) elaborating the 'O' antiphons of the Christmas liturgy, hailing Christ under his liturgical titles — key of David, cornerstone, dayspring, Emmanuel. The eleventh lyric's 'Eala Earendel' inspired Tolkien's mythology of Eärendil.
plot_or_argument: The lyrics, addressed to Christ or spoken in his voice, celebrate the mystery of the Incarnation: the closed door of the Virgin, the cornerstone rejected by builders, the light rising in darkness, the bridegroom come to Zion. Each lyric meditates on a title or antiphonal image and prays for the coming of the Lord.
narrative_structure: A lyric sequence of twelve meditations on the antiphons, framed by the liturgical season of Advent.
principal_characters: Christ; Mary; the faithful of Zion
literary_form: religious lyric (sequence) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; lyric intensity rather than narrative continuity.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book as the opening of the composite poem 'Christ' (fols. 8a-14a); the antiphons are those sung at vespers in the week before Christmas.
literary_significance: The great Advent poetry of the period; source of the 'Earendel' passage that founded Tolkien's legendarium.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; once attributed to Cynewulf with the rest of the trilogy, but the Advent lyrics are now regarded as separate and unsigned.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 8a-14a.

title: Christ II (The Ascension)
description: The middle section of the Exeter Book 'Christ' (427 lines), signed by Cynewulf: a meditation on the Ascension based on Gregory the Great's homily, celebrating Christ's 'leaps' — from heaven to earth, into the womb, onto the cross, into the tomb and hell, and back to the throne of glory.
plot_or_argument: The poet meditates on the Ascension as the climax of Christ's career of 'leaps' (from the Song of Songs image of the beloved leaping upon the mountains), recounts the apostles' grief and the angel's promise of return, interprets the 'gifts of men' of Psalm 67 (the talents of wisdom and craft distributed to mankind), and closes with a vision of the Last Judgment and Cynewulf's runic signature and prayer.
narrative_structure: A homiletic meditation in verse: Gregory's leaps, the ascension narrative, the catalogue of gifts, eschatological conclusion, and runic signature.
principal_characters: Christ; the apostles; the angel
literary_form: religious lyric/meditation in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; the signature passage is elaborately wrought.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 14a-20b) between the Advent lyrics and Christ III; based on Gregory the Great's Homily 29 on the Gospels.
literary_significance: The classic Old English treatment of the Ascension; its gifts-of-men passage inspired The Gifts of Men and Fortunes of Men.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 14a-20b.

title: Christ III (The Judgment)
description: The final section of the Exeter Book 'Christ' (798 lines): the grandest poetic vision of the Last Judgment in Old English, in which Christ appears on the cross at doomsday, the elements dissolve, the sinners and the blessed speak their laments and thanks, and the poem closes on the joys of heaven.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the sudden coming of the Judge, the blast of trumpets, and the conflagration of the world — the sea, the stars, the mountains consumed; Christ, still bearing the wounds and the cross, separates the blessed and the damned, who speak in antiphonal choruses (the damned reproaching their sins, the blessed thanking Christ for the 'thirst on the cross'); the poem ends with the blessed entering the heavenly city.
narrative_structure: A visionary sequence: theophany, cosmic dissolution, the dialogue of blessed and damned, and the entry into heaven; the speeches are organized in paired laments and thanksgivings.
principal_characters: Christ the Judge; the blessed; the damned
literary_form: religious narrative (eschatological vision) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre of sustained grandeur; celebrated descriptions of the dissolving cosmos.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 20b-32a); the judgment scenes draw on patristic and homiletic eschatology.
literary_significance: The summit of Old English eschatological poetry; a major source for later medieval judgment literature.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; formerly assigned to Cynewulf with the rest of the trilogy.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 20b-32a.

title: Guthlac A
description: A poem of 818 lines on the Mercian hermit Guthlac of Crowland: his arrival in the fenland retreat, his battles with the demons who tempt and torment him, and his vindication by the apostle Bartholomew. Based on Felix's Latin Vita, the poem turns the saint's spiritual warfare into heroic combat in the native manner.
plot_or_argument: The young Mercian warrior Guthlac, renouncing war, takes up the solitary life in the fens of Crowland; demons assault his cell, carry him to the gates of hell, and accuse him of pride; the apostle Bartholomew commands his release and the devils obey; Guthlac returns victorious, and the poem closes with his death and the angels' reception of his soul.
narrative_structure: A hagiographical epic in the heroic mode: renunciation, the demonic wars (a psychomachia in narrative form), heavenly vindication, and death; speeches dominate the central combat scenes.
principal_characters: Guthlac; the demons; Bartholomew; the angels
literary_form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre, with the diction of heroic combat applied to spiritual warfare.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 32b-44b); source: Felix of Crowland's Vita Sancti Guthlaci (c. 730-740).
literary_significance: The classic vernacular treatment of the hermit-warrior and of the fenland as spiritual battlefield.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 32b-44b.

title: Guthlac B
description: A poem of 561 lines on the death of St Guthlac of Crowland, from the Exeter Book: the saint's illness, his last conversation with his servant Beccel, and the ascent of his soul, which flies like a bird to heaven. Distinct from Guthlac A in style and emphasis, it is one of the most tender poems in the corpus.
plot_or_argument: Stricken with his final illness, Guthlac instructs his disciple Beccel, foretelling his own death on the seventh day; his soul departs like a bird to the heavenly home, and a light shines over the fen; Beccel, instructed to tell his sister Pega, buries him and the poem closes with a prayer. The poet's meditation on death — 'death is no man's friend' — frames the narrative.
narrative_structure: A single, intimate deathbed narrative: prophecy, farewell dialogue, and the ascent of the soul, framed by prologue and prayer.
principal_characters: Guthlac; Beccel; Pega; the angels
literary_form: religious narrative (hagiographical) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; gentler and more meditative than Guthlac A.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 44b-52b); source: Felix's Vita Sancti Guthlaci.
literary_significance: The finest Old English poem on the death of a saint; its bird-image for the soul's flight is among the period's most memorable figures.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; distinct authorship from Guthlac A is generally accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 44b-52b.

title: Soul and Body I and II
alternative_titles: The Soul's Address to the Body
description: A pair of related poems (Vercelli Book I, 166 lines; Exeter Book II, 121 lines) in which the soul, revisiting its decaying body once a week, reproaches it for the sins of the flesh and foretells the torments of judgment. The earliest English body-and-soul debate, ancestor of a long medieval tradition.
plot_or_argument: The damned soul, forced to revisit its corpse, addresses the silent body: 'Where are the riches you gathered? The hall you feasted in?' — enumerating the body's pleasures and their price in hell, the worms and the fire; the Exeter version closes with a brief address to the blessed soul by contrast. The debate's later fortunes run through the Middle English 'Desputisoun bitwen the Bodi and the Soule' to the danse macabre.
narrative_structure: A monologue of reproach and warning, spoken by the soul to the body at the grave; the two versions differ in length and ending.
principal_characters: the Soul; the Body; (in II) the blessed soul
literary_form: religious debate poem in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre.
historical_context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 101v-103v) and the Exeter Book (fols. 98a-100a); the genre derives from Latin and homiletic sources.
literary_significance: Inaugurates the body-and-soul debate tradition that runs through Middle English literature.
bibliographical_notes: Vercelli Book, fols. 101v-103v; Exeter Book, fols. 98a-100a.

title: Maxims I and II
description: Two collections of gnomic verse — Maxims I in the Exeter Book (204 lines, in three sections) and Maxims II in British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i (66 lines) — assembling traditional wisdom about the order of the world: what befits a king, a warrior, a woman, a tree, frost, the sea, and the road; 'wyrd goes as it shall'.
plot_or_argument: The maxims proceed by association through the natural and social orders: the king belongs in the hall, the sword in battle, the hawk on the glove, the frost to the earth, the mind to wisdom; each thing is 'in its place' — a poetic articulation of the period's sense of a world arranged by custom and providence.
narrative_structure: Catalogue structure: strings of 'X shall be / belongs to' gnomes, organized by loose association rather than narrative.
principal_characters: none
literary_form: wisdom poetry (gnomic verse) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre in short, proverb-like units.
historical_context: Maxims I: Exeter Book (fols. 88b-92b); Maxims II: London, British Library, Cotton MS Tiberius B.i (with the Menologium, c. 1050).
literary_significance: The fullest repository of Old English gnomic wisdom and of the period's sense of natural and social order.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book; Cotton MS Tiberius B.i.

title: The Fortunes of Men
description: A poem of 98 lines cataloguing the fates that befall men — one dies young, one by the sword, one from a fall, one on the gallows; the hawk dies, the wolf mourns, the singer is praised — closing with the assurance that God apportions all gifts. A companion to The Gifts of Men.
plot_or_argument: The poem surveys the deaths and destinies of men (and, in an admired passage, of a hawk), then turns to the arts — one man learns song, one harp, one the law — and concludes that the Measurer shapes each man's lot, bestowing craft, wealth, and wisdom as he will.
narrative_structure: A double catalogue (fates, then gifts) closed by a doxological gnome on divine providence.
principal_characters: none
literary_form: wisdom poetry (catalogue) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 87a-88b), following Widsith.
literary_significance: A finely crafted example of the catalogue poem and of the period's providential view of human diversity.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 87a-88b.

title: The Exeter Book Riddles
description: A collection of some ninety-five riddles in the Exeter Book, ranging from the majestic (the swan, the iceberg, the storm, the bookworm) to the bawdy double entendres (the onion, the key, the churn), all spoken in the first person by their subjects — the largest surviving body of riddles in any early medieval vernacular.
plot_or_argument: Each riddle presents an oblique first-person self-description — 'I am a wonderful creature...' — inviting the reader to name the hidden subject; subjects include weapons, tools, animals, natural forces, writing, and domestic objects, with several deliberately suggestive 'obscene' solutions masking innocent ones.
narrative_structure: A sequence of independent enigmas, likely arranged by the compiler in thematic groups; the collection ends with a famous series of double-entendre riddles.
principal_characters: the speaking objects (swan, iceberg, bookworm, onion, key, etc.)
literary_form: riddle (enigma) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; the riddles vary from four lines to over a hundred.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 101a-115a and elsewhere); the genre descends from the Latin enigmata of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
literary_significance: The cornerstone of the English riddle tradition; a unique window onto the everyday and the marvellous in Anglo-Saxon imagination.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the collection may include compositions by several poets over centuries.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 101a-115a (with related items).

title: The Metrical Psalms of the Paris Psalter
description: A verse translation of Psalms 51-150 preserved in the Paris Psalter (Bibliothèque nationale de France, lat. 8824), accompanying the prose translation of Psalms 1-50. Once attributed to King Alfred, the verse psalms are now regarded as anonymous tenth- or eleventh-century work; they constitute the largest single body of Old English psalmody.
plot_or_argument: The psalms are rendered in fluent alliterative verse, expanding the biblical text with traditional poetic diction; the collection provides the fullest surviving example of Old English liturgical translation in verse.
narrative_structure: A continuous psalter translation, psalm by psalm, in the versified mode.
principal_characters: David (as psalmist); God
literary_form: metrical psalter in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre of a relatively plain, expository kind.
historical_context: Preserved in the Paris Psalter (Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS lat. 8824), a mid-eleventh-century manuscript with Latin text and Old English translation in parallel columns; the first fifty psalms are in Alfredian prose.
literary_significance: The fullest English verse psalter before the late Middle Ages; important for the study of vernacular liturgy.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the older attribution to Alfred is not now accepted, though the prose portion may be Alfredian.
bibliographical_notes: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS lat. 8824.

title: The Metrical Charms
description: A group of verse charms against illness, theft, and misfortune, preserved mainly in eleventh-century medical manuscripts (the Lacnunga and related collections). The charms blend Christian prayer with pre-Christian incantation — most famously the Nine Herbs Charm, invoking Woden as the healer of herbs, and Wið færstice, against a sudden stabbing pain caused by a 'mighty woman's' riding.
plot_or_argument: Each charm prescribes words and actions for a specific ill: the Nine Herbs Charm enumerates the nine sacred herbs and their powers against poison and infection, invoking Woden's victory with nine glory-twigs; Wið færstice fights the elf-shot with a spear-image and a boiled herbal drink; others protect bees from swarming, fields from blight, and travellers from harm.
narrative_structure: Prescriptive lyric sequences: invocation, narrative of the ill or its cure, and ritual instruction, often in verse alternating with prose directions.
principal_characters: Woden (in the Nine Herbs Charm); the healer; the malevolent powers
literary_form: metrical charm (incantation) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre, often irregular; incantatory repetition.
historical_context: Preserved in London, British Library, Harley MS 585 (the Lacnunga), the Old English Herbarium manuscripts, and other medical compilations; the pre-Christian elements survived within Christian manuscripts.
literary_significance: The richest vernacular evidence for Anglo-Saxon folk medicine and for the survival of Germanic ritual in a Christian culture.
bibliographical_notes: London, British Library, Harley MS 585 (Lacnunga); Royal 12 D.xvii; and related medical manuscripts.

title: Solomon and Saturn I and II
alternative_titles: The Dialogue of Solomon and Saturn
description: Two wisdom dialogues in which Solomon, the biblical master of wisdom, contends with Saturn, the legendary Chaldean sage, over questions of fate, prayer, and the powers of the Pater Noster — its letters imagined as armed warriors assailing the devil. The poems are the most extravagant of the Old English wisdom tradition.
plot_or_argument: In Solomon and Saturn II, the sages debate the powers of the Pater Noster: each letter becomes a warrior with a specific weapon against the fiend ('P has a golden rod and fights the devil...'); the poem surveys the poem's battles against evil in a fantasia of personified letters. Solomon and Saturn I concerns the praise of the Pater Noster and the books it governs, with a runic passage on the letter R.
narrative_structure: Question-and-answer dialogue in the wisdom-contest tradition, elaborated with the allegorical letter-warfare of the Pater Noster passages.
principal_characters: Solomon; Saturn; the personified letters of the Pater Noster
literary_form: wisdom poetry (dialogue) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; dense, sometimes eccentric diction.
historical_context: Preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MSS 41 and 422; the dialogues draw on apocryphal Solomonic and computistical lore.
literary_significance: The wildest flights of the Old English wisdom tradition; central to the study of Anglo-Saxon learned imagination.
bibliographical_notes: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MSS 41 and 422.
